summary: Varun Beverages makes and sells PepsiCo drinks such as Pepsi, Mountain Dew, Sting, Tropicana and Aquafina water in India and several other countries, under licence from PepsiCo. It is also starting to sell snacks and beer in parts of Africa.
description: PepsiCo owns the brands, and Varun Beverages (VBL) holds the right to make and sell them in set territories. VBL buys the flavour concentrate from PepsiCo and turns it into finished drinks in its own plants. It fills bottles, stores them in depots, and delivers them to distributors and shops, where it often places glass-fronted fridges to keep drinks cold. It covers 26 states and 6 union territories in India and nine other countries with franchise rights, and about two-thirds of its revenue comes from India. Its financial year is the calendar year, January to December.
money: VBL earns money by selling cases of drinks to distributors and shops, which sell them to consumers. Its main costs are the sugar, PET (a common plastic) chips, which are granules moulded into bottles, and flavour concentrate it buys, plus staff, electricity, trucks and fridges placed in shops. Plants and fridges also cost money to buy and run over many years. Most sales fall in the hot months. A customer's payment is revenue, not profit.
customers: Consumers drink the products, but VBL's direct buyers are distributors and shops, reached through its own sales and distribution teams across urban, semi-urban and rural areas. PepsiCo is not a customer. It licenses the brands to VBL and supplies the concentrate.
drivers: How many cases it sells, especially in the hot months, the cost of sugar and PET chips, and how fully its plants, depots and fridges are used.

groups.title: Fizzy drinks
groups.examples: Pepsi, Pepsi Zero, Mountain Dew, Sting, Seven-Up, Mirinda and Evervess.
groups.explanation: The report calls these carbonated soft drinks, which are drinks with bubbles. They are PepsiCo's brands, made and sold by VBL under licence.

groups.title: Juice-based and sports drinks
groups.explanation: These are the report's non-carbonated drinks. The report also lists licensed energy drinks as a category.

groups.title: Packaged drinking water
groups.explanation: VBL fills and sells Aquafina water in bottles, which the report counts among its non-fizzy drinks.

groups.title: Snacks
groups.examples: Cheetos made in Morocco and Zimbabwe, and PepsiCo snacks sold in Zimbabwe and Zambia.
groups.explanation: The report says VBL began making and distributing PepsiCo snacks in parts of Africa in 2025. It is a new line beside drinks.

groups.title: Beer test in Africa
groups.examples: Carlsberg beer in selected African territories.
groups.explanation: VBL signed an exclusive distribution agreement with Carlsberg to test-market the beer. A test market means selling in a few places first to see whether demand justifies more.

basics.title: What does it mean to be a PepsiCo franchisee?
basics.text: PepsiCo owns the brands and licenses another company to make and sell them in an agreed territory. The report says VBL is the second-largest PepsiCo franchisee in the world outside the United States.

basics.title: What are fizzy and non-fizzy drinks called in the report?
basics.text: The report uses the shorthand carbonated soft drinks (CSD) for fizzy drinks and non-carbonated beverages (NCB) for drinks such as juice, sports drinks and water.

basics.title: Why does the year run from January to December?
basics.text: VBL reports on a calendar year. It says the drinks business is seasonal, with most sales in summer, so it is best to judge performance over a full year, not one quarter.

basics.title: What is a visi-cooler?
basics.text: The report uses the word for the refrigerated display units VBL provides to shops. In plain terms, it is a fridge with a glass front that keeps drinks cold where shoppers can see them.

steps.title: Buy the ingredients
steps.text: PepsiCo supplies the flavour concentrate. VBL buys sugar and PET chips, and the report says it signs advance purchase contracts to steady the price.

steps.title: Make and fill
steps.text: Plants mix the drink and fill bottles. The report says it has been adding new plants and facilities for its own inputs.

steps.title: Store and deliver
steps.text: Depots and distribution centres hold stock, and distributors and VBL's own sales teams deliver to shops in cities, towns and villages.

steps.title: Keep drinks cold in shops
steps.text: VBL places visi-coolers in shops. The report says electricity supply and refrigeration differ by country and are a challenge.

steps.title: Bill and collect
steps.text: Revenue (what VBL bills), profit (what is left after costs) and cash received are different things. The report says trade receivables carry no interest and the credit period generally ranges from 0 to 120 days.

specifics.title: PepsiCo owns the brands, VBL runs the operations
specifics.text: The report says PepsiCo provides brands, concentrates and marketing support, while VBL runs manufacturing, supply and capital spending. The India bottling and trademark agreement has been extended to 30 April 2039.

specifics.title: Two-thirds of revenue is from India
specifics.text: The report says India contributed about 67 percent of its net operating revenue in 2025. The rest comes from countries including Nepal, Sri Lanka, Morocco, Zambia, Zimbabwe and South Africa, each with its own currency and weather.

specifics.title: VBL builds its own fridge supply
specifics.text: The report says it formed a joint venture to manufacture visi-coolers and refrigeration equipment in India, so it depends less on outside suppliers for the fridges it places in shops.

specifics.title: Moving beyond soft drinks
specifics.text: In 2025 VBL began making and distributing snacks in parts of Africa and signed a beer distribution test. On 21 December 2025 it agreed to buy Twizza, a South African soft-drink maker, and took control of it on 18 March 2026. Twizza was merged into VBL's South African subsidiary from 1 August 2026.

watch: Does a rainy summer leave Varun selling fewer drinks?
Summer is a busy season, so weak sales then can affect the full year.
Compare sales volumes by quarter and by India and international markets over several years, with the weather commentary.
How secure are the PepsiCo agreements in each territory?
VBL depends on PepsiCo for brands and concentrate. The report warns that termination or less favourable renewal could affect profit.
Read the notes on franchise agreements and their end dates in the annual report, and look for any change in the list of territories.
How are the newer African territories doing?
South Africa and the Democratic Republic of Congo were added recently, and the report lists integration of new territories as a risk.
Compare the international commentary and volume growth with the previous year, including the cases VBL reports from Twizza, and watch how South Africa is run after the Twizza merger.
How do sugar and PET chip prices change the cost of each case?
These are the main inputs the report names, and prices move.
Compare cost of materials as a share of revenue each year and read the note on commodity price sensitivity.
Are low-sugar and no-sugar versions growing?
The report links health trends and sugar rules to demand, and shows how much of volume comes from lower-sugar drinks by brand.
Read the table of lower-sugar volume by brand and compare it with the previous year's report.
risks: Agreements with PepsiCo could end or renew on worse terms
The report says VBL relies on its agreements with PepsiCo and that termination or less favourable renewal could affect profit.
Health rules and taxes on soft drinks
The report says products could be targeted by discriminatory taxes and packaging waste rules, and new consumer health rules could follow.
Consumers moving away from sugary drinks
The report says failing to adapt to health trends, or to explain the health effects of soft drinks, could harm demand.
The report says it needs a continuous supply of PET chips and sugar and that prices are volatile. It signs advance purchase contracts, but a price jump still raises the cost of every case.
context: December 2025 to August 2026: Twizza bought and merged in South Africa

On 21 December 2025 a South African subsidiary of VBL agreed to buy 100 percent of Twizza, a South African soft-drink maker, subject to regulatory approvals. VBL's results release of 27 April 2026 says it completed the purchase through that subsidiary and that Twizza became a subsidiary from 18 March 2026. The company's 30 October 2026 results release says Twizza was merged into that subsidiary from 1 August 2026 and that Twizza added 15.3 million cases in July to September 2026. Press reports of 31 March 2026 (Business Report, quoting Standard Bank, adviser to the seller) also describe the sale as complete after regulatory approvals.

financialNotes.title: How to read the figures
financialNotes.text: These are consolidated figures, meaning Varun Beverages and its subsidiaries and joint ventures in India and abroad together, for the calendar year to 31 December 2025. The company reports one business segment, drinks, so it does not show profit by brand or country. Its sales are seasonal. Profit after tax is the profit left after all expenses and tax. Other income includes a ₹228 crore gain from currency movements. It is an accounting gain, and the cash flow statement treats a currency gain of this kind as not received in cash. Profit is also after ₹13.9 crore at the parent company for the government's new Labour Codes, revised labour laws, which raised its retirement-pay provision.

stepsTitle: From flavour concentrate to a cold bottle.

quick.title: What it does
quick.text: It makes and sells PepsiCo drinks, with some snacks and beer in parts of Africa, in India and several other countries.

quick.title: Who pays
quick.text: Distributors and shops buy the drinks. Consumers are the final drinkers.

quick.title: How it earns
quick.text: It sells cases of bottled drinks and water at prices set to cover its own costs, and earns more in hot summers.

quick.title: What it spends on
quick.text: Sugar, plastic for bottles, flavour concentrate, staff, trucks and the fridges placed in shops.

helps.title: A long partnership and wide territory
helps.text: The report describes more than three decades with PepsiCo and franchise rights across 26 states and 6 union territories in India, which gives VBL the rights to make and sell these brands across a large area.

helps.title: Markets where fewer people buy yet
helps.text: The report says it is present in relatively underpenetrated markets, meaning places where fewer people drink these brands, with favourable demographics, a growing population and a warm climate.

helps.title: Capacity already built
helps.text: The report says capacity built over recent years is now translating into operating leverage, meaning more sales can be handled without a matching rise in costs. That depends on volumes reaching the plants.

hurts.title: A weak summer hurts the whole year
hurts.text: The report says the soft drinks business is seasonal, with the bulk of sales in summer. In 2025 it said weather-related disruptions in India during the peak summer season held volume growth back.

hurts.title: New territories take time to pay off
hurts.text: The report lists business viability risk as failing to integrate newly acquired territories or gain efficiencies from them. New plants and territories cost money before they earn it.

hurts.title: Plants and fridges need steady spending
hurts.text: The report says investment in route-to-market expansion and visi-cooler deployment remains critical, so money goes out for equipment before the sales it enables arrive.
